lessonTitle: Formulating Answerable Questions: PICO and Search Strategies

blocks.text: A mother asks whether the probiotic yoghurt her four-year-old has been given will stop antibiotic-related diarrhoea. Typing 'probiotics diarrhoea' into a search engine returns thousands of pages, none of which answers whether it works, in children, taking antibiotics. The answer starts with a better question, not a better search engine.

blocks.markdown: Evidence-based practice has five steps: **ask** an answerable question, **acquire** the best evidence, **appraise** it, **apply** it with the patient, and **assess** the result. A vague question ('tell me about probiotics') yields a vague search. A structured question tells you which study design to look for and which words to search.

blocks.title: PICO
blocks.text: A clinical question is framed as **P**opulation or patient (who, with what condition), **I**ntervention (or exposure, test, or prognostic factor), **C**omparison (the alternative: placebo, usual care, another treatment, or no exposure) and **O**utcome (what matters to the patient, and when). Some questions add **T**ime or **S**tudy design (PICOT, PICOS). Diagnostic questions replace intervention with the index test and comparison with the reference standard; prognosis questions use a prognostic factor.

rows: Age, condition, setting; not so narrow that nothing exists
Children aged 1-12 years receiving a course of oral antibiotics
The specific treatment, dose class or exposure
Oral probiotic taken during the antibiotic course
Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea within 2 weeks of the course
blocks.caption: Turning a clinical problem into the four PICO elements.

blocks.title: Writing a PICO question
blocks.prompt: Rewrite the mother's concern as a PICO question and identify the most suitable study design.

steps.text: Separate the problem from the context: the patient is a child on antibiotics, the proposed intervention is a probiotic, and what the family cares about is whether diarrhoea occurs.
Fill in each element, with the comparison made explicit.
steps.latex: P=\text{children on antibiotics},\; I=\text{probiotic},\; C=\text{no probiotic or placebo},\; O=\text{diarrhoea during or after the course}

steps.text: Write one sentence: 'In children taking a course of antibiotics (P), does a probiotic (I) compared with placebo or no probiotic (C) reduce the incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (O)?'
This is a therapy question, so the best primary study is a randomised controlled trial, and the best summary is a systematic review of such trials.

blocks.answer: A well-formed therapy question: in children on antibiotics, does a probiotic versus placebo reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea? Look first for systematic reviews of RCTs.

blocks.markdown: **Searching.** Once the question is framed, convert each PICO element into a *concept* and search each concept with both **controlled vocabulary** and **free-text** words. Key bibliographic databases are MEDLINE (via PubMed or Ovid), Embase (strong for drugs and European journals), the Cochrane Library (including CENTRAL, a register of trials) and CINAHL (nursing and allied health). Trial registries and grey literature reduce the risk of missing unpublished results.

blocks.title: Controlled vocabulary versus free text
blocks.text: **Controlled vocabulary** is a curated thesaurus in which indexers assign standard subject headings to each record: MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) in MEDLINE, Emtree in Embase. A heading captures synonyms, so one term finds papers that use different words, and 'explode' also retrieves narrower headings beneath it. **Free-text** words found in titles and abstracts catch new terms and records not yet indexed. A sensitive search uses both. Truncation (for example `child*`) retrieves word endings; quotation marks search an exact phrase. Exact symbols differ between databases.

rows: Combine synonyms within one concept (probiotic* OR Lactobacillus)
Use sparingly; it can drop relevant records
Study-design filters apply the question's best design
blocks.caption: Boolean operators and search tools. Parentheses control the order in which they are applied.

blocks.title: Building a search strategy
blocks.prompt: Build a search for the probiotic question for MEDLINE-style syntax, and explain the logic.

steps.text: Concept 1 (population): combine the subject heading and free-text synonyms with OR.
steps.latex: \text{(Child[MeSH] OR child* OR paediatric* OR pediatric*)}

steps.text: Concept 2 (intervention): similarly combine the heading and free text for the probiotic.
steps.latex: \text{(Probiotics[MeSH] OR probiotic* OR Lactobacillus OR Saccharomyces)}

steps.text: Concept 3 (outcome): diarrhoea, in both British and American spellings, with its heading.
Join the three concepts with AND, so every record mentions all of them, then optionally apply a randomised-trial design filter. Add database-specific syntax and field tags as needed.
Test the strategy against a few papers you already know are relevant; if they are missing, add synonyms or headings. Record the databases, dates and exact strings so that the search is reproducible.

blocks.answer: (Child terms) AND (probiotic terms) AND (diarrhoea terms), with MeSH and free text combined by OR within each concept and an optional RCT filter.

blocks.latex: \text{Recall}=\frac{\text{relevant records retrieved}}{\text{all relevant records}},\quad \text{Precision}=\frac{\text{relevant records retrieved}}{\text{all records retrieved}},\quad NNR=\frac{1}{\text{Precision}}
blocks.caption: Search performance. High recall (sensitivity) is the priority for a systematic review; the number needed to read (NNR) is the screening workload per relevant record.

blocks.markdown: **Best design by question type.** The design that answers a question with least bias depends on the question. A therapy question needs a comparison with random allocation; a diagnostic question needs a comparison with a reference standard in a representative sample; a prognosis question needs follow-up of people with the condition from a similar point in the disease; a harm question needs an exposed group and a comparison group, but harms that are rare or delayed often can only be studied by observational designs.

rows: Cohort study, with greater risk of confounding
Cross-sectional accuracy study with all patients receiving index test and reference standard
Case-control accuracy study (prone to spectrum bias)
Harm or aetiology (does exposure cause it?)
Randomised trial if ethical and feasible, otherwise cohort study
blocks.caption: Matching question type to design; systematic reviews of the best design sit above single studies.

blocks.title: Common errors in framing
blocks.text: A question without a comparison cannot be answered ('is exercise good for back pain?' - compared with what?). Outcomes that are surrogate or vaguely worded ('improves') should be replaced by patient-important outcomes with a time frame. Too narrow a population may retrieve nothing; too broad a one retrieves unusable heterogeneity. Searching a single database or only free text can miss relevant studies.

points: Frame a clinical question as PICO (population, intervention, comparison, outcome); the question type determines the study design to look for.
Search each PICO concept with controlled vocabulary (MeSH, Emtree) and free-text synonyms, combined with OR within a concept and AND between concepts.
Use several databases such as MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library, and record the strategy; judge it by recall and precision.
Therapy: RCT; diagnosis: cross-sectional accuracy study; prognosis: inception cohort; harm: cohort or case-control when trials are unethical or infeasible.

questions.stem: A trainee asks: 'In adults with chronic low back pain, is a supervised exercise programme better than usual GP care for pain at 6 months?' Which part of the question is the comparison?

options.text: A supervised exercise programme
Adults with chronic low back pain
Usual GP care
Pain at 6 months

distractorRationale.c: Correct: the alternative against which exercise is judged is the comparison.
distractorRationale.d: This is the outcome with its time point.

questions.explanation: The comparison is what the intervention is measured against, here usual GP care. The adults with chronic low back pain are the population, the exercise programme is the intervention and pain at 6 months is the outcome. Stating the comparison explicitly is what makes the question answerable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best-formed answerable clinical question?

options.text: Is diabetes education good?
What is known about diabetes?
Does education help patients with diabetes mellitus more than doing nothing?
In adults with type 2 diabetes, does a structured education programme compared with standard care improve HbA1c at 12 months?

questions.correctOptionText: In adults with type 2 diabetes, does a structured education programme compared with standard care improve HbA1c at 12 months?

distractorRationale.a: This lacks a population, comparison and outcome.
distractorRationale.b: This is too broad to guide a search or study design.
distractorRationale.c: The comparator is stated, but no outcome or time frame is given, so it cannot be answered precisely.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: it names a population, intervention, comparison and a measurable outcome with timing.

questions.explanation: A well-built question identifies who, what is done, what it is compared with and which outcome is measured and when. The correct option contains all four, whereas the others omit the outcome, comparison or population and would give unfocused searches.

questions.stem: When building a database search for a question about 'heart attack', which strategy is best?

options.text: Use only free-text 'heart attack' because headings are unnecessary
Combine the controlled heading with free-text synonyms (for example myocardial infarction, heart attack) using OR
Use NOT to remove any record mentioning 'angina'
Link all synonyms with AND to maximise relevance

questions.correctOptionText: Combine the controlled heading with free-text synonyms (for example myocardial infarction, heart attack) using OR

distractorRationale.a: This misses papers that use other terms such as myocardial infarction.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: OR within a concept combines the heading and different wordings, increasing sensitivity.
distractorRationale.c: NOT may exclude relevant records and is not a way to combine synonyms.
distractorRationale.d: AND would require every term in each record, making the search too narrow.

questions.explanation: Synonyms for the same concept are joined with OR, and different concepts are joined with AND. Controlled headings such as MeSH pull in records that use various words, while free-text terms find papers that are new or not yet indexed, so using both gives the most sensitive search.

questions.stem: A student searches only MEDLINE for a systematic review of a drug treatment. Why is this a weakness?

options.text: Systematic reviews should search only grey literature
A search of one database cannot use Boolean operators
A single database may miss relevant studies, so Embase, the Cochrane Library and registries should also be searched
MEDLINE does not contain randomised trials

questions.correctOptionText: A single database may miss relevant studies, so Embase, the Cochrane Library and registries should also be searched

distractorRationale.a: Grey literature supplements, not replaces, bibliographic databases.
distractorRationale.b: Boolean operators can be used in any database.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: coverage differs between databases, and a comprehensive search needs several sources.
distractorRationale.d: MEDLINE does index trials; the problem is incomplete coverage.

questions.explanation: Different databases index different journals and use different vocabulary, so relying on one risks missing studies and introducing bias. Systematic reviews search several databases (for example MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL), trial registries and reference lists, and they report the strategies used.

questions.stem: A clinician wants to know which features at diagnosis predict whether patients with a new stroke will be independent at 1 year. Which design best answers this prognosis question?

options.text: A cross-sectional survey of current stroke survivors
A prospective inception cohort followed for 1 year
A randomised trial of a drug
A qualitative interview study

questions.correctOptionText: A prospective inception cohort followed for 1 year

distractorRationale.a: A one-time snapshot of survivors cannot show who would become independent from diagnosis.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: patients are enrolled at a similar early point and followed forward to the outcome.
distractorRationale.c: There is no intervention to allocate; the question is about prediction.
distractorRationale.d: This explores experience; it does not estimate prognosis.

questions.explanation: Prognosis requires follow-up of people from a defined starting point, so an inception cohort is ideal. A cross-sectional sample of survivors misses those who died or did poorly early on, which would bias estimates of outcome.

questions.stem: A researcher wishes to know whether a new rapid blood test accurately detects a bacterial infection in febrile children, compared with culture. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: A case-series of children with a known positive culture only
A cohort of children followed for 10 years
A cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study in which consecutive febrile children receive both the rapid test and culture
A randomised trial of two antibiotics

questions.correctOptionText: A cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study in which consecutive febrile children receive both the rapid test and culture

distractorRationale.a: Without test-negative and disease-free children, accuracy cannot be calculated.
distractorRationale.b: Long follow-up does not compare the test with a reference standard.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: all patients receive the index test and reference standard in a representative sample.
distractorRationale.d: This addresses treatment, not test accuracy.

questions.explanation: Diagnostic questions need the index test compared with a reference standard in people in whom it would be used. Recruiting consecutive patients and testing all with both methods allows sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios to be calculated while limiting spectrum and verification bias.

questions.stem: A search for a systematic review retrieves 1,250 records, of which 25 are relevant. Calculate the number needed to read (NNR), defined as 1/precision, as a number of records per relevant record.
questions.explanation: Precision is $25/1250=0.02$ (2%), so $NNR=1/0.02=50$ records must be screened to find each relevant record. High-sensitivity systematic review searches typically have low precision, so a large screening workload is accepted in exchange for not missing studies.

questions.stem: Reviewers have a benchmark set of 32 papers that they know are relevant. A new search strategy retrieves 28 of them. Calculate the recall (sensitivity) of the search as a percentage and consider whether it is acceptable for a systematic review.
questions.explanation: Recall is the proportion of known relevant records that the search found: $28/32=0.875$, i.e. 87.5%. Four of 32 known papers were missed, so the strategy should be improved (more synonyms, headings or databases) before it is accepted for a systematic review.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacist asks whether routine vitamin D supplementation in older care-home residents reduces fractures. Write a PICO question, state the best study design, and outline a search strategy including controlled vocabulary, Boolean logic and at least two databases.
markingGuide: Population: older adults living in care homes
Intervention: vitamin D supplementation; Comparison: placebo or no supplementation; Outcome: fractures within a stated period
Best design: randomised controlled trial; best summary: systematic review of RCTs
Concepts combined with AND; synonyms within each concept combined with OR
Controlled vocabulary (MeSH, Emtree) plus free-text terms and truncation
At least two databases (for example MEDLINE and Embase, plus the Cochrane Library or CENTRAL); record and test the strategy
questions.explanation: A good answer names each PICO element, matches the therapy question to randomised trials, and builds a reproducible search that joins synonyms by OR and concepts by AND using both headings and free text across several databases.

questions.stem: For each of the following question types, state the best primary study design and one reason, and say one alternative design if the best is impractical: (a) the effect of a treatment, (b) the accuracy of a diagnostic test, (c) the prognosis of a condition, (d) a rare harm from a drug.
markingGuide: Therapy: randomised controlled trial, because random allocation balances confounders
Diagnosis: cross-sectional accuracy study in consecutive patients, with a reference standard for all
Harm: RCT if ethical, but cohort or case-control study for rare or delayed harms
Alternatives: cohort for therapy; case-control for rare harm; registries or retrospective cohorts for prognosis
Mention that the design must fit the question, not the other way round
questions.explanation: Each question type has a design that minimises bias for that purpose: randomisation for therapy, a reference standard in a representative sample for diagnosis, inception cohorts for prognosis, and observational designs when harms are rare or delayed. A candidate should explain why, not only name the design.
